title: NASA Artemis III Will Launch Three Rockets to Test Two Lunar Landers
excerpt: The 14-day Earth-orbit mission in summer 2027 will dock Orion with Blue Origin's Blue Moon and SpaceX's Starship, clearing the way for a 2028 lunar landing.
body:
• Artemis III, targeted for summer 2027, will launch three heavy-lift rockets in about two weeks: Blue Origin's New Glenn, NASA's Space Launch System and SpaceX's Starship.
  • The 14-day low Earth orbit mission will test Orion docking with both the Blue Moon Mark 2 and Starship landers, instead of landing on the Moon.
  • Crew is NASA astronauts Randy Bresnik, Frank Rubio and Andre Douglas, plus ESA astronaut Luca Parmitano.
  • For readers tracking the timeline: a successful test keeps Artemis IV on track for the first crewed lunar landing since 1972 in 2028.

NASA has detailed a flight plan for Artemis III that uses three separate rockets to test two competing lunar landers in Earth orbit, as the agency works to return astronauts to the Moon's surface in 2028.

The mission, outlined at Kennedy Space Center on October 23, will last about 14 days and stay a few hundred miles above Earth. It replaces the original plan for Artemis III to be the first crewed landing since Apollo 17 in 1972. That landing now belongs to Artemis IV.

Three launches in one campaign

The sequence starts with Blue Origin. Its New Glenn rocket will launch a test version of the Blue Moon Mark 2 lander from Launch Complex 36A at Cape Canaveral into a circular orbit about 273 miles above Earth. NASA says the lander can wait in orbit for up to 30 days, giving schedulers flexibility if later launches slip.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=_LgzKaJ5PgI

NASA will then launch its Space Launch System from pad 39B with the Orion capsule and four astronauts. Orion will move to a circular orbit near 345 miles, rendezvous with Blue Moon on about day three, and dock. The crew will open the hatch, enter the lander cabin and check atmosphere, pressure, software, flight controls and life support over about two days.

After Orion undocks, SpaceX will launch a Starship Version 3 test vehicle from pad 39A with a docking system at its nose. Orion will dock with Starship for about two hours on day eight. The crew will not enter Starship. NASA wants data on how Orion handles, communicates and undocks with a second, very different architecture.

"We're launching three of the most powerful rockets in the world and undertaking what is likely the most complicated launch campaign ever undertaken."

— Jeremy Parsons, NASA Artemis Program Manager

NASA describes the dual approach in its Artemis III mission overview as a way to demonstrate how Orion interfaces with two commercial lander designs in a single mission, before committing to one for a landing.

Why NASA changed the mission

Administrator Jared Isaacman reshaped the Artemis roadmap earlier this year, adding the 2027 orbital test and pushing the landing to 2028. The change followed schedule pressure on both landers. Engadget and NASA reporting note the program is about three months behind an internal plan, and Blue Origin must restore a Florida launch pad damaged in a May hot-fire explosion before New Glenn flies again, targeted for the end of this year.

https://www.instagram.com/reel/De2t82PPyx9/

SpaceX faces its own list: a propellant-transfer demonstration in early 2027, landing-leg and airlock tests, and a Florida Starship pad. Neither lander has flown with crew or docked with a crewed spacecraft.

Beyond docking, the crew will test the Orion Crew Survival System suits, run human research and science experiments, and evaluate how astronauts could carry out health assessments without direct contact with mission control — a skill needed for lunar surface work.

What happens next

If Artemis III flies in summer 2027, both companies are expected to fly uncrewed landing demonstrations — SpaceX in late 2027 and Blue Origin in early 2028 under current plans — before Artemis IV attempts a landing near the lunar south pole. NASA has not yet chosen which lander will carry that crew, saying it will decide on readiness and schedule data from Artemis III.

The stakes extend beyond the United States. India’s space programme, and Indian-origin researchers and engineers working across NASA centres and contractors, track Artemis as the framework for future lunar science and commercial work. A proven docking test in 2027 would be the clearest signal yet that the 2028 landing date is credible.
